extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science and history of ideas (readers of Bacon)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and critical analysis of Francis Bacon's notions of 'Form', his Method of Exclusions, and his treatment of Final Causes as set out in the Novum Organum and related writings. The page explains Bacon's intended meanings, limitations, and practical consequences for scientific method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Form' as essence / differentia / definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon uses 'Form' in passages where it can be replaced by words like 'essence', 'differentia', or 'definitio vera' (e.g. 'forma vera', 'differentia vera', 'definitio vera', 'ipsissima res').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'form' may be understood as the aggregate of primary or underived attributes whose enumeration (or 'differentia') constitutes the definition or essence of a class, substance, or quality. When expressed in words, the important/characteristic part of the definition is the differentia which distinguishes the term from other members of the same genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Form' as law / cause / determination of act
rubrics_metrics.description: In other passages Bacon treats 'Form' as a 'lex actus jive motus' — the law or determination of the pure act which orders and constitutes a nature (e.g. 'leges fundamentales et communes quae constituunt formas').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here 'form' is the law of development/manifestation/production of a given quality or body; taking into account pre-existing conditions plus the law yields the fuller conception of 'cause'. Thus 'form' can be read as the causal law governing a phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence (practical) of essence and cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically, knowledge of the essence (aggregate of primary attributes) and knowledge of the cause are equivalent: given the primary attributes, the phenomenon follows; given conditions and the law, one can produce the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence underlies Bacon's sanguine expectation that knowing simple natures would allow artificial production of substances by superimposing them. It is a practical aim of his method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Exclusions (Rejectio sive exclusiva) as primary inductive tool
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the 'form' of a simple nature Bacon's 'Method of Exclusions' consists in ascertaining with what natures the given nature is not connected; if all but one are excluded, the remaining nature is the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is to reject singular natures which are not present when the given nature is present, or which appear in inverse relation (increase when given nature decreases etc.). After proper rejection and exclusions, a 'forma affirmativa, solida, et vera' should remain. In practice Bacon saw this as the cornerstone of his system but acknowledged its practical difficulty and incompleteness under current knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for auxiliary aids: Tables and praerogativae instantiarum
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon requires 'Tables' and 'praerogativae instantiarum' and other 'aids of the intellect' to complete the Exclusiva and to assist the method of exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusiva is not perfect at early stages; auxiliary classificatory and exemplary devices are necessary to approach the ideal exclusion and to 'clear up our conceptions of the simple natures.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of single cause (unity) and its limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's enquiry presumes that every phenomenon has only one cause (one set of conditions) — i.e. there is one simple nature which, if found, is the 'Form' of the given nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption is critiqued: phenomena may have plurality of causes (different sets of conditions at different times). Mill's critique and the possibility of multiple sufficient conditions render Bacon's criteria and exclusions sometimes vitiated; the same effect need not always be due to the same cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining which of two concomitant natures is form/ cause: temporal precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: When two natures are invariably connected, nothing within mere coexistence determines which is the Form of the other except the notion that one is a limitation of a more general nature; practically, the determination of cause vs effect rests on establishing which precedes in time in individual instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertainment of temporal precedence in particular instances resolves whether one nature is cause and the other effect; Bacon implicitly leans on causal (temporal) relations as well as genus/species relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer affirmative induction when inductive requirements satisfied
rubrics_metrics.description: If the connection between two phenomena satisfies all the requirements of the inductive methods (as stated in Novum Organum ii.15), one is justified in affirming a causal relation without performing exhaustive exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While exclusions eliminate alternatives, affirmative inductive evidence that meets the stated criteria can and should be used to assert causation; exhaustive exclusion is rarely attainable in current states of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about confusing laws of coexistence with laws of succession
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a danger of conflating laws of coexistence (uniformities of co-presence) with laws of succession (causal sequences); derived qualities may follow from collocation of primary qualities even if the time involved is infinitesimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must distinguish co-existence regularities from succession (causal) regularities; failure to do so can mislead the attribution of form/ cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Final Causes: excluded from physics but legitimate in metaphysics/natural theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon rejects Final Causes from Physics (maintaining efficient/material/formal causes are proper to physics) and transfers Final Causes to Metaphysics (Natural Theology), warning that their intrusion into physics expels enquiry into real physical causes ('Tractatio Causarum Finalium in Physicis inquisitionem Causarum Physicarum expulit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final causes are not denied as true or worthy of speculation, but they must remain within metaphysical/theological inquiry; if misapplied to physics they become sterile and divert inquiry. The author also notes that certain sciences (e.g., physiology) legitimately use functional/adaptive reasoning and that modern theories (e.g., evolution) change how one may interpret adaptation and finality.
